entities.name: José Manso de Velasco, 1st Count of Superunda
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
José Manso de Velasco, 1st Count of Superunda, stands as a pivotal figure in the administrative history of 18th-century Spanish America, serving as Governor of Chile (1737–1744) and later as the 17th Viceroy of Peru (1745–1761). Born in 1689 in Torrecilla en Cameros, Spain, his career exemplified the ascendancy of professional military officers in colonial governance under the Bourbon reforms. His leadership was particularly defined by his robust efforts to consolidate royal authority, implement infrastructural improvements, and, most famously, rebuild the viceregal capital after a catastrophic natural disaster.

During his governorship of Chile, Manso de Velasco founded numerous cities, including Rancagua, Curicó, Talca, and Copiapó, strategically aimed at populating the territory, improving communications, and asserting Spanish control over the frontier regions, particularly against indigenous Mapuche resistance. His administrative acumen earned him the viceregal appointment to Peru. There, his tenure was immediately tested by the devastating 1746 Lima-Callao earthquake and tsunami, which destroyed Lima and virtually annihilated Callao. Manso de Velasco orchestrated an unprecedented reconstruction effort, meticulously planning the new urban layout of Lima and implementing strict building codes, while also establishing the Royal Hospital of San Andrés and reorganizing the city's defenses.

His long viceregency, the second-longest in Peruvian history, marked a period of significant administrative reorganization and economic consolidation. He streamlined tax collection, combatted contraband trade, and sought to curb the power of the local Creole elite, aligning colonial governance more closely with the centralizing tendencies of the Spanish Crown. Though recalled in 1761 due to accusations of laxity during the Hapsburg-Bourbon conflicts, his reforms laid crucial groundwork for the later, more radical Bourbon changes under figures like José de Gálvez and Charles III.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: José Manso de Velasco's tenure as Viceroy of Peru dramatically reshaped Lima following the 1746 earthquake and implemented crucial Bourbon administrative reforms across the Andean region, strengthening Spanish imperial control and urban development. His actions had a lasting impact on the physical and political landscape of colonial South America.
